finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token with loose == against attacker-supplied $token; if $token is PHP boolean true (e.g. from a JSON body), the check passes for any non-empty stored token and the victim's password is replaced without the token. On PHP < 8, integer 0 also matches.
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password_loose (reset.php:2), attacker-typed via JSON body; precondition: a pending resets row exists for the victim email.

trace.note: row fetched by attacker-chosen $email; exists if a reset was requested for that address
password replaced with attacker-chosen hash for the email

finding.guards_checked: $db->quote($email) prevents SQL injection but not this bypass; no type check on $token; no expiry check. Function has no caller in the supplied directory, so reachability is unconfirmed.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:3 fetches the row with a parameterized-style $db->quote($email), which stops SQL injection but not the type juggling. reset.php:4 uses loose == with no type check on $token, and nothing in the file checks expiry. The sibling reset_password (reset.php:12-20) uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, but it is a separate function and is not on this path.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: reset.php:4 does `$row['token'] == $token`, and a boolean true from the attacker passes that check, so reset.php:5-6 replace the password. Whether an anonymous attacker can reach it is undecided, because the only match for reset_password_loose in the directory is its definition at reset.php:2 and no caller exists here to show an exposed route.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are never consumed, expired or invalidated. The same email/token pair can reset the password repeatedly, and older outstanding tokens are never revoked because fetch() takes an arbitrary first row with no ORDER BY.
finding.source: Any previously valid email/token pair (leaked or forwarded reset email, log exposure, shared mailbox).

trace.note: SELECT token by email, fetch() returns first row; no expiry, used-flag or ORDER BY
no DELETE or flag update, so the token remains valid for the next call

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals is constant-time and the (string) cast is correct; no expiry, single-use enforcement, or invalidation of older tokens. Mitigated only if another code path deletes the row after success, which is not in the supplied directory.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:13-14 only fetches and compares the token; reset.php:15-17 updates the password and returns true, with no DELETE, used-flag, or expiry check anywhere in reset.php. The directory contains only reset.php, so no other cleanup path is visible.
verdict.reason: reset_password() at reset.php:13-17 accepts any matching token for the email and never invalidates it, so the same token can be replayed to reset the password again. The attacker must already hold a valid email/token pair, so this is anonymous-with-token rather than privilege escalation, and the claim that older tokens are "never revoked" is muddled because line 13 only ever checks the first returned row. The core missing single-use and expiry enforcement at reset.php:16 is real.

finding.claim: The loose reset function compares the token with == (early-exit), leaking matching-prefix information via timing; the strict function uses hash_equals.
finding.source: Attacker-supplied $token guesses for a known email.

trace.note: strict version uses hash_equals for comparison

finding.guards_checked: Strict version is constant-time. No attempt limit or rate limiting in either function. Impact is small unless the token is short or unthrottled.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:4 compares with == and reset.php:14 uses hash_equals, as claimed. Nothing in the file rate-limits attempts or constant-time-compares the loose path. Any caller that reaches reset_password_loose (reset.php:2) with an attacker-chosen $token gets the comparison.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: reset.php:4 uses == (early-exit on the first differing byte) while reset.php:14 uses hash_equals, and no guard in the file blocks an anonymous attacker who knows the email from guessing tokens, so the flaw is real but low severity, since a network timing oracle against a long random token is practically infeasible. The more serious issue on the same line is PHP loose-comparison type juggling: two numeric-looking strings such as "0e123" and "0e456" compare equal under ==, so a crafted token can match without knowing the real value.
